title: Graphs
tagline: BFS, DFS, Dijkstra, Union-Find — and the four representations interviewers expect you to know cold.
intro:
A graph is a set of **vertices** connected by **edges**. It's the most general data structure here — trees and linked lists are just special cases — and it models almost any 'things and relationships' problem: maps, networks, dependencies, friendships, states and transitions. The skill interviewers test is recognising a problem *is* a graph problem, then picking the right traversal.

The good news: a small toolkit covers the vast majority. **BFS** for shortest paths in unweighted graphs and level exploration. **DFS** for connectivity, cycle detection, and topological order. **Dijkstra** for shortest paths with non-negative weights. **Union-Find** for grouping and dynamic connectivity. Knowing when each applies — and how to represent the graph — is 90% of the battle.

This module covers the representations, the BFS/DFS templates with a visited set, topological sort, Dijkstra, and Union-Find — plus the trap of forgetting to mark nodes visited.
objectives: Represent a graph as an adjacency list, matrix, or implicit grid
Run BFS for shortest path in an unweighted graph
Run DFS for connectivity, cycle detection, and topological sort
Apply Dijkstra for shortest paths with non-negative weights
Use Union-Find (DSU) for connectivity and grouping
Always track visited nodes to avoid infinite loops in cyclic graphs

signals: Things connected by relationships: maps, networks, prerequisites, friends
"Shortest path / fewest steps" in an unweighted graph → BFS
"Number of islands / connected components / can you reach" → DFS or Union-Find
"Course schedule / build order / dependencies" → topological sort
antiSignals: Acyclic hierarchy with a single root → it's a tree, use tree methods
Negative edge weights → Dijkstra fails, use Bellman-Ford
Tiny fixed structure → maybe direct simulation is clearer

sections.heading: The big idea in plain words
sections.body:
A graph is a map: cities are dots (nodes) and roads are lines (edges) connecting them. A question like 'what's the fewest stops between two cities?' is answered by exploring outward in rings - first everything one stop away, then everything two stops away, like ripples spreading on a pond. That ring-by-ring search is BFS.

Example: counting islands in a grid. Treat each piece of land as a city joined to its neighbouring land cells. Start on one land cell and 'flood' outward to every connected land cell, marking each as visited. Every fresh flood you have to start counts as one more island - simple, and you touch each cell only once.

sections.heading: Vocabulary and representations
sections.body:
| Term | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Directed / undirected** | Edges one-way (a→b) or two-way (a—b) |
| **Weighted** | Edges carry a cost/distance |
| **Cyclic / acyclic** | Has a loop or not (a DAG is a directed acyclic graph) |
| **Degree** | Number of edges touching a vertex |
| **Connected component** | A maximal set of mutually reachable vertices |

Four ways to store a graph — pick by density and access pattern:

| Representation | Space | Edge lookup | Best for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Adjacency list** | O(V+E) | O(degree) | most problems (sparse graphs) |
| **Adjacency matrix** | O(V²) | O(1) | dense graphs, fast edge tests |
| **Edge list** | O(E) | O(E) | Kruskal, simple iteration |
| **Implicit grid** | — | neighbours = 4/8 cells | matrix/maze problems |

Adjacency list is the default. Grid problems are graphs in disguise: each cell is a vertex, edges go to adjacent cells.

sections.heading: Which algorithm? (decision flow)
sections.body:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
  A["Graph problem"] --> B{"Weighted edges?"}
  B -- No --> C{"Shortest path / fewest steps?"}
  C -- Yes --> D["BFS"]
  C -- "Connectivity / components / order" --> E["DFS or Union-Find"]
  B -- "Yes, non-negative" --> F["Dijkstra (min-heap)"]
  B -- "Yes, negative allowed" --> G["Bellman-Ford"]
  E --> H{"Dependencies / ordering?"}
  H -- Yes --> I["Topological sort"]
```

sections.heading: BFS and DFS templates
sections.body: Both explore the graph; the difference is the order. **BFS** uses a queue and explores in expanding rings — so the first time it reaches a node is via the fewest edges, giving shortest paths in unweighted graphs. **DFS** uses recursion (or a stack) and dives deep before backtracking — ideal for connectivity and ordering. Both **must** track a visited set, or a cycle sends them into an infinite loop.

DFS connectivity (count islands)

callouts.text: Mark a node visited when you ENQUEUE it in BFS, not when you dequeue it — otherwise the same node gets added to the queue multiple times before it's processed.

sections.heading: Topological sort (dependency ordering)
sections.body: On a **DAG**, a topological order lists every vertex before the vertices that depend on it — the classic 'course schedule' / 'build order' problem. Kahn's algorithm (BFS): compute each node's in-degree, start from the zero-in-degree nodes, and repeatedly remove a node and decrement its neighbours' in-degrees. If you can't remove all nodes, the graph has a **cycle** (no valid order exists).

codeExamples.label: Topological sort (Kahn's algorithm)
codeExamples.code:
from collections import deque

def topo_sort(n, edges):
    adj = [[] for _ in range(n)]
    indeg = [0] * n
    for a, b in edges:        # a -> b (a before b)
        adj[a].append(b)
        indeg[b] += 1
    q = deque(i for i in range(n) if indeg[i] == 0)
    order = []
    while q:
        node = q.popleft()
        order.append(node)
        for nxt in adj[node]:
            indeg[nxt] -= 1
            if indeg[nxt] == 0:
                q.append(nxt)
    return order if len(order) == n else []   # [] means a cycle

sections.heading: Dijkstra and Union-Find
sections.body:
**Dijkstra** finds shortest paths from a source in a graph with **non-negative** weights. It's BFS with a min-heap: always expand the cheapest-so-far node. It fails with negative edges (use Bellman-Ford there).

**Union-Find (Disjoint Set Union)** tracks which vertices are in the same component under a stream of 'union these two' operations, with near-O(1) `find` and `union` using path compression and union by rank. It's the go-to for 'number of connected components', 'redundant connection', and Kruskal's MST.

| Algorithm | Use | Complexity |
| --- | --- | --- |
| BFS | unweighted shortest path | O(V+E) |
| DFS | connectivity, cycles, topo | O(V+E) |
| Dijkstra | non-negative weighted shortest path | O((V+E) log V) |
| Union-Find | dynamic connectivity, grouping | ~O(α(n)) per op |

callouts.text: Grid/maze problems ARE graph problems. Treat each cell as a vertex with edges to its 4 (or 8) neighbours — then BFS gives shortest path, DFS counts regions, no explicit graph build needed.

interviewTalking: First, declare it's a graph and name the representation: "I'll model this as an adjacency list — or, since it's a grid, each cell is a node with edges to its four neighbours." Then justify the algorithm by the question: "Fewest steps in an unweighted graph means BFS, because the first time BFS reaches a node it's via the shortest path." Always mention the visited set up front — 'to avoid revisiting in a cyclic graph' — and give O(V+E) (or O((V+E) log V) for Dijkstra).
commonMistakes: Forgetting the visited set → infinite loop on cyclic graphs
Marking visited on dequeue instead of enqueue in BFS → duplicate queue entries
Using DFS for shortest path in an unweighted graph (BFS is the one that guarantees it)
Running Dijkstra with negative edge weights (it gives wrong answers — use Bellman-Ford)
Building an O(V²) adjacency matrix for a sparse graph that fits an O(V+E) list
Topological sort without detecting the cycle case (order shorter than V)
complexityNotes: BFS and DFS are O(V+E) time and O(V) space. Topological sort (Kahn's) is O(V+E). Dijkstra with a binary heap is O((V+E) log V). Union-Find with path compression and union by rank is near-constant, O(α(n)), amortised per operation.
